source.title: Bigger Is Safer: Provable Robustness in In-Context Learning Scales with Capacity
source.authors: Di Zhang; Ningxu Zhang; Zimeng Liu

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or garbling; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies scaling of robustness to adversarial shifts in in-context learning, not held-out cross-entropy loss, loss extrapolation, compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, or the other listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The reported scaling results concern safe perturbation radius and the number of in-context examples needed under adversarial shifts, not the loss-scaling behavior in the claim. Those distinct robustness findings are recorded with versions ["none"]. Cited results from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: The paper studies how adversarial in-context-learning robustness (safe perturbation radius, extra examples needed) scales with attention head dimension in linear Transformers, plus a label-flipping stress test on 21 pretrained LLMs. It reports no held-out pretraining loss sweeps, loss extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, or shape-versus-loss results. Its 'scaling laws' are robustness-capacity relations, a different construct, so it tests none of V1–V7. It does not cite either original source.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors prove and synthetically confirm that the safe radius scales as the square root of head dimension and that the extra examples needed scale as ρ². They present real-LLM results as qualitative evidence, with ICL capability as a prerequisite and diminishing returns for very deep models. They say nothing about loss scaling.
record.recipe_differences: The study derives a Wasserstein distributionally robust bound for ICL and tests safe radius under synthetic perturbations and label-flipping in demonstrations. It does not use the held-out-loss sweeps or compute-optimal allocation methods in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported robustness depends on task and ICL competence, context size, head dimension and depth; the real-model test uses label-flipping as a proxy rather than an exact Wasserstein-2 adversary.

fits_no_version.finding: Synthetic linear Transformers show safe radius rising with head dimension, with log-log slope 0.453 (r=0.991). Real LLMs (0.5B–3B) give slope 0.276 against total parameters.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adversarial ICL safe radius grows roughly as a power of model capacity.

fits_no_version.finding: The fitted adversarial sample-tax coefficient a(m) falls from about 1195 to 675 as m rises from 16 to 256.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger capacity reduces the extra in-context examples needed under adversarial shift.

fits_no_version.finding: In real LLMs, safe radius is non-monotonic in parameter count (Qwen 3B > 7B; Cerebras 590M > 1.3B; Pythia 1.4B > 6.9B). ICL competence is a prerequisite.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adversarial ICL robustness depends on architecture and ICL competence, not raw parameter count alone.

fits_no_version.finding: On sentiment, the 0.5B model is about 18x less sensitive to in-context examples than on the safety task, which the authors call pseudo-robustness.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Measured ICL robustness depends on whether the task requires genuine in-context learning.

record.problems: The paper's main theory assumes linear self-attention and Gaussian task distributions. The authors describe real-LLM evidence as qualitative, use label-flipping rather than an exact Wasserstein-2 adversary, and note a sparse head-dimension range and possible effects of nominal accuracy. These limitations concern its robustness findings; it does not provide evidence on the claim's loss-scaling outcomes.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant held-out cross-entropy, parameter/token/compute loss-sweep, or compute-optimal-allocation results are reported. Other experiments about compression, deployment recommendations, and bound verification were not included because they do not bear on the claim's loss-scaling versions.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute; not measured.
Extrapolation of loss from small to large runs; not measured.
Compute-optimal parameter and token split; not studied.
Effect of depth or width on loss at fixed parameters. Depth and head-dimension effects are reported only for robustness, not loss.
Loss power laws in other modalities or regimes; not measured.
Downstream performance versus scale. Safe radius is a robustness score, and clean accuracy is reported only incidentally, not analysed as scaling.
Dependence of loss-scaling exponents on setup or fitting choices; not studied.

record.verdict_notes: The term 'scaling laws' here refers to robustness-capacity relations, not pretraining loss. R3 duplicates R4 with the wrong subject. All other rows correctly carry versions ['none'].

Extrapolation of held-out loss from small runs to much larger runs.
Effects of architecture details on held-out loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability of downstream task performance from model scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of loss-scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup and fitting choices.
